title: The GOP’s Midterms-Money Advantage Has Its Limits
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
American politics is saturated with cash, and each election cycle seems to set new spending records—and yet, with the midterms in the home stretch, neither party thinks it has enough money
The irony is nearly as rich as the biggest donors
Filings released this week show that $1 billion was spent on the campaign in the first two weeks of October alone
This year’s elections are expected to be the most expensive midterms in U.S. history, beating 2022 —which beat 2018, which beat 2014, and so on

This will not surprise anyone who lives in a state or district with a competitive race this fall. (I’m sure I can still recite the Senate Leadership Fund’s ad attacking the North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper, weeks after it stopped running .) Democratic and Republican voters don’t agree on a ton these days, but they’re united on one position: There’s too much money in politics
Ask officials and candidates in both parties, though, and you’ll hear that they don’t have nearly enough
Democrats are feeling fairly confident about capturing the House and are getting more hopeful about their chances at winning the Senate, yet officials worry they don’t have enough cash

The party got a big boost on Monday, when Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire former New York mayor and presidential candidate, announced that he would pour $80 million into helping Democrats before Election Day
Republicans came into this election with a huge money advantage, and they continue to have millions available to spend
Even so, major GOP organizations are finding themselves having to make unpleasant choices to stop spending in races that seem to be slipping away from them

Senate Leadership Fund, which is the top Republican PAC supporting Senate races, didn’t spend any money on TV ads last week to support the Georgia candidate Mike Collins , who is expected to lose to Senator Jon Ossoff

SLF had already pulled back from helping the Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina. (To make matters worse, President Trump hosted a rally with Whatley on Tuesday in Greenville, where he said that Cooper is “going to become your senator, and it’s crazy.”) One reason both parties are scrambling for money is that the map has shifted
As Trump’s political position deteriorates and he drags GOP candidates along with him, races that once seemed like foregone conclusions are now real battles
Democrats worry that they don’t have enough funding to match their potential
Republicans, by contrast, are having to play defense in what they thought were safe seats
SLF has moved money from North Carolina to Kansas, a state where a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race since 1932 but where Adam Hamilton is posing a real threat to Senator Roger Marshall

Republicans are also finding that their decision to squeeze new gerrymanders out of some states before this election has been costly: Districts that they expected to be easy Republican pickups are now close combat

Punchbowl News recently reported that although the GOP has a lock on five of 14 new districts, “Republican candidates and super PACs have spent nearly $100 million on ads trying to flip the other nine districts” since September 1
Another reason is that not all money is created equal
Some Democratic candidates are very well funded

The Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, for example, raised $64 million in the third quarter of the year alone—the highest total for any candidate in that period ever. (Because Texas has so many voters and so many media markets, it’s an expensive place to campaign.) But Democratic committees, including top PACs, are much more strapped

This is partly because the sitting president’s party always has a leg up in fundraising, but it’s also because many donors have grown disillusioned with the Democratic Party, upset with strategic decisions in the 2024 presidential loss, chaotic management of the Democratic National Committee since, and uninspiring leadership by elected officials
Republican candidates (such as Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton) have relatively little money on hand, but committees and PACs are still flush
Much of that money comes from independent-expenditure groups, such as super PACs
An analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice finds that these groups spent $2 billion through the end of September, leaning heavily toward Republicans
The single largest donor is Elon Musk, who has spent $366 million this cycle alone
But one disadvantage of independent-expenditure groups is that they have to pay higher rates for advertisements than candidates
That’s perhaps the dominant theme of the late campaign: Republicans have lots of money, but they’re not necessarily getting much bang for their buck
At this stage in the campaign, the time to build serious infrastructure, such as canvassing operations, is past
Money can buy a lot of advertising, but TV time is either booked up or more expensive
Besides, Republicans have already spent lavishly to fill airwaves, websites, and mailboxes with ads
So far , they don’t seem to be seeing much impact : Races either remain close or appear to be shifting even further toward Democrats
Understanding why the GOP candidates are stalled is not difficult

Voters are upset about high prices, especially for fuel, and they are turned off by a president who is dismissive of their affordability concerns, distracted by vanity projects, and bogged down in an unpopular and inflationary war in Iran
Trump’s super PAC has $164 million left to spend , but as any orthodox Lennonist knows, money can’t buy you love

title: Welcome to the Valley of Pain
excerpt: This week could go down as the worst in the history of cybersecurity
body: This week could go down as the worst in the history of cybersecurity

On Wednesday, news emerged about two major vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by 70 percent of websites, which prompted governments, hospitals, and companies around the world to take digital services offline as a precaution
There have already been millions of attempts to exploit these weaknesses
But the PHP vulnerabilities were just the most attention-grabbing in a series of alarming revelations
Security flaws in, or successful hacks of, several major software products and platforms—including some used by Netflix, PayPal, Walmart, and other big names—were announced that same day
Yesterday, Quest Diagnostics, which runs lab tests for a third of American adults each year, disclosed that it, too, had been breached

When I asked Sam Rubin, a senior vice president at the cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks, about the potential fallout from yet another hack—this one of the cloud platform Railway, which is used by Intuit and MGM Resorts, among others—he paused. “I didn’t see that one,” Rubin said. “It’s been quite a busy week.” [ Read: ‘If anything happens to this guy … everyone is screwed’ ] Yet what’s most alarming about the past few days is that by next year, this stretch of incidents—which some security experts are calling “Black October”—may be remembered as normal, or even tame. “It’s going to feel like, over and over and over again, we’re finding more and more bugs in very critical pieces of software,” Matthew Prince, the CEO of the internet infrastructure and security company Cloudflare, told me. “This story, which feels unique and fresh right now—in a few months, it’s going to feel like we get one of these every week.” Prince said he knows of still more vulnerabilities that will be announced in the near future

For the next year or two, if not longer, the internet is going to feel a bit touch and go, and more dangerous than we’ve come to expect. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling” for a while, Prince said
There’s a decades-long backlog of bugs in software written without much review or scrutiny—which was more or less fine so long as there was a very small number of skilled hackers

Over the past two decades, companies, governments, and individuals have been lulled into a false sense of security: Most people don’t think twice about punching credit-card numbers into the website of a local restaurant or gift shop, or forking over a home address and phone number in just about any customer survey
But the internet was always a dangerous place
AI agents can now be deployed as a cheap and near-infinite hacker army

In just the past couple of months, Rubin said, open-source models—which can be downloaded for free and used without restrictions—have become very good at finding vulnerabilities and automating attacks
In turn, the amount of malicious cyber activity has spiked
More websites will be defaced, more personal information will be stolen, and ransomware will proliferate

Rubin told me that the internet is entering a “valley of pain.” When I posed the concern that this is the new normal to Adam Meyers, a senior vice president at the cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, he told me, “I think it’s going to get a lot worse, actually.” Consider, for instance, another set of vulnerabilities disclosed this week, to the program Node.js

This software, which executes JavaScript code for dynamic webpages, is widely used by Fortune 500 companies, as well as in programs developed with AI. “These are the things the web runs on,” Meyers said

Because of how the platform is used, compromising just one software product that uses Node.js could infect tens of thousands of other organizations, Rubin said, in what is known as a “supply-chain attack.” And the skill threshold for launching cyberattacks has become almost absurdly low: CrowdStrike tied a spate of cyberattacks on South Korean banks late last month to a 26-year-old in China. “After he got access to all the data, he turned around and asked AI, ‘How do I monetize this? Where can I sell this?’” Meyers told me

He “didn’t know what he was doing.” Meyers said CrowdStrike is detecting “a new agentic adversary”—that is, an AI-powered hacking operation—“every two hours.” Navigating this will require rapid and tremendous coordination from basically every sector
For instance, the vulnerabilities in PHP were discovered months ago by a consortium of AI and cybersecurity firms

Then, “very quietly, for the last several months, we and other industry partners worked to effectively put in place protections,” Prince said—basically, temporary shields until the weaknesses could be fully addressed

But “not everybody uses CloudFlare, and not everybody is quick to patch their software.” Some of the cybersecurity experts I’ve spoken with are optimistic about AI: Eventually, they say, AI will be used to find and address many of the major cybersecurity flaws, and the internet will become much safer overall

But before then, we may be stuck in a terrible limbo. “This is going to last as long as it takes to rewrite and secure the billions of lines of code that have always had these vulnerabilities,” Alex Stamos, the chief information-security officer at the AI company Cognition and a former chief security officer at Facebook, told me
And even as cybersecurity experts rush to leverage AI to save the internet, the technology is introducing plenty of new problems
All vibe-coded apps, for starters, are very likely to contain security flaws

And at a time when people need to be more vigilant about their digital hygiene, multiple cybersecurity experts brought up the widespread adoption of AI assistants with more than a hint of scorn; as Rubin put it: “Our peers are using Muse and giving it carte blanche to use your credit card.” The internet is becoming a wilder place, and the path to secure it may require, in essence, a sort of pruning. “You’ll likely see more companies take services off the internet when they don’t need to be there,” depreciating old webpages and forms so they can’t be targeted, Dan Guido, the CEO of the cybersecurity firm Trail of Bits, told me

Individuals might be encouraged to delete unused browser extensions, he added, so that there are “fewer pieces of software that can access your data.” People in general need to be “more discerning of the companies they work with,” Stamos said, and “you’re just not gonna be able to assume every site you use is secure.” That Pokémon trading-card website, fantasy-sports platform, or birding forum you use could be hacked for a password you’ve reused elsewhere, or a credit-card number, or worse
Other advice I heard: Don’t host your own email client instead of Gmail
Don’t host your own file system at home instead of using the cloud
Google and Dropbox have the resources to defend against an onslaught of AI hacks, and you don’t

If, eventually, we do find and shore up all of the cybersecurity vulnerabilities out there, the result could be a more open web, where anybody can use widely available AI tools to run security checks at any time and you’ll feel safer sharing your personal information again
But another possibility is an even more centralized internet, where only services and websites developed by large software providers are deemed trustworthy and reliable
The internet needs new walls to defend against AI-powered attacks
But in turn, we might also feel walled in.

title: The DEI Language That’s Doing More Harm Than Good
excerpt: Last week, Senator Edward Markey published a social-media post seeking interns for his Boston office
body: Last week, Senator Edward Markey published a social-media post seeking interns for his Boston office

He wrote that “BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans, and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply.” Outrage quickly followed: Critics treated the post not as a straightforward attempt to encourage diversity in job applications, but rather as a discriminatory signal that white men would be disadvantaged in hiring
The Manhattan Institute’s Christopher Rufo called the help-wanted ad an open violation of civil-rights law and urged a federal probe

The former Trump Justice Department appointee Theo Wold wrote that a goal of Democrats is to ensure that young white men “have no opportunities to find gainful employment.” One response to Markey stated, “If you are a young White man struggling financially, I understand your frustration with the Iran conflict and gas prices, but you must understand that this is the official hiring policy of the entire corporate world if democrats return to power.” Because X rewards inflammatory retorts more than intellectual rigor, these particular claims of racial grievance are easy for skeptics to dismiss as sensationalism
Urging certain groups to apply for a job is not proof of hiring discrimination against others
Some groups that Markey’s post mentioned, such as gay people, veterans, and the working class, include lots of white men
There is overwhelming evidence that the Democratic Party’s goal is not “no opportunities” for white men, and that corporations are not a left-identitarian monolith
Still, setting all falsehoods and exaggerations aside, Democratic elected officials have long been more likely than Republicans to favor policies that consider race and sex in employment decisions

These policies sometimes result in credible claims of discrimination against white and/or male candidates: Large nonprofits , major cities , multinational corporations, and prestigious law firms have all lost court cases involving employment discrimination against white people or men, or altered their employment practices under pressure from federal or state agencies that enforce civil-rights laws

Republicans generally treat such discrimination as a bigger problem than Democrats, even as most Americans—including a majority of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents— reject preferential treatment in hiring and promotions for favored groups

Populist-right partisans are probably correct that they have a political opportunity in going after any left-leaning political, academic, or business elites who push such policies. [ Read: Democrats can’t let go of racial preferences. ] The issue may prove especially potent for men in Generation Z
As recently as 2019, just a third of young men perceived some discrimination against men in America
In 2025, 51 percent of young men perceived it
Those feeling aggrieved by Markey’s words should bear in mind that, at 80, his views about race were formed before the civil-rights era
For most of his life, identity politics in Congress favored straight white men

Perhaps he still perceives that all groups other than white men need reassurance, and would be surprised that young white men today have any such need. (His office did not respond to my request for comment.) But older legislators need to grasp that efforts to diversify organizations, many of which focus on new hires, mean that Gen Z has a unique experience of the job market

Exposing white men in this cohort to language that seems to treat them differently from other groups is particularly unwise––they are especially primed to infer discriminatory intent whether or not it is being implied

Cheryl Kaiser, a psychology professor at the University of Washington, researches how “well-intentioned organizational diversity initiatives create unintended consequences.” She told me in an email that, although outreach to particular identity groups is distinct from restricting hiring to those groups, “the mere presence of a diversity signal, not the signal’s actual impact in hiring decisions, can increase White Americans’ concerns that they’ll face racism.” (In fact, several federal and state laws prohibit discrimination based on race, sex, or other protected characteristics—and these are laws that are intended to protect everyone, not just women or people of color.) In scholarship published in 2021, Kaiser and her co-authors found that “simply exposing White Americans to organizational diversity signals” increased their perception of a bias in hiring against white men
That perception occurred “even with clear evidence of White advantage within the organization, a less-qualified White candidate, or abundant promotion opportunities for all employees

Nor was it limited to people predisposed toward biased beliefs: the effect did not depend on participants’ endorsement of group-based hierarchy or their level of racial ingroup identification.” In another research paper, from 2015 , Kaiser and her co-authors found that the mere presence of pro-diversity signals “cause White male mock job applicants to experience cardiovascular stress as well as anticipate experiencing discrimination when applying for jobs at these companies.” Of course, the fact that people perceive discrimination does not mean they are actually being discriminated against
And if diversity language were effective in contributing to more equitable hiring outcomes, even while upsetting a few overly sensitive sorts, there would be a strong case for retaining it

But Kaiser believes that “the types of diversity signals that cause backlash often do very little to effectively diversify the workplace.” Research she published in 2020 found that “racial minority employees sometimes see organizational diversity signals as overstating real commitment, which is linked to feeling less able to fit in or thrive.” Often, then, diversity signals confound all assumptions: “They don’t produce the hiring outcomes critics fear, they don’t produce the trust or inclusion benefits supporters are aiming for, and yet they still trigger the perceptual backlash described above,” Kaiser told me
To meaningfully reduce resentment, grievance, and reactionary identitarianism among young white men, Democrats should adopt rhetoric that unambiguously clarifies a commitment to equal opportunity
For decades, the political right insisted that racial preferences were immoral and illegal, and that diversity efforts should be restricted to outreach
Now they’re treating mere outreach as proof of illegal discrimination
But as Kaiser’s research shows, diversity rhetoric can have unforeseen effects

White identitarians would exist even in a world without bias of any sort in recruitment or hiring––but using language that fuels white identity politics, as Markey’s language did, is political malpractice that’s bad for Americans of all races, no matter how well intentioned it might be
Even if one argues that diversity advocates shouldn’t have to change how they communicate in order to avoid backlash, the reality seems to be that they do
As is often the case in politics, social progress requires forging broad coalitions of people who often disagree
That requires an understanding of psychology, attentiveness to possible sensitivities, and, yes, even compromise
Outreach that values diversity and inclusion is still possible

In 2015, the social psychologist Wiebren Jansen and co-authors found that “including the cultural majority group in an organization’s diversity approach” can help white men with a high need to belong feel included, and can increase support within organizations for diversity efforts
Senator Elizabeth Warren’s approach to recruiting interns is a good example of inclusive language

Her call for applications uses familiar and simple language, describing her office as “an equal-opportunity employer” that does not discriminate based on “race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, age, genetic information, disability, or uniformed service.” Warren “encourages all individuals from all backgrounds to apply.” Whether you’re Black or white or trans or gay or working-class or a veteran, if you are wondering whether people like you belong, that approach leaves no ambiguity: You’re encouraged to apply. “All individuals” are.

title: The Armageddon Economy
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube It can feel like an existential moment right now—one where many tech leaders are both warning against and acc
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube It can feel like an existential moment right now—one where many tech leaders are both warning against and accelerating the destructive forces of AI
But Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that this could also be a turning point toward building something better
The authors of End Times Fascism talk with Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel about runaway wealth, the politics of AI, and how to prepare if the tech-bloated market crashes
The following is a transcript of the episode: Astra Taylor: You know, are there ways to deal with a crash that lets the people who’ve perpetrated this, like, eat the downside
Like, could this be an opportunity to get rid of some of the excess wealth and the inequality in this moment? Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain
AI researchers are quitting in droves, and they’re worried that what they’re building might kill us all
It’s easy, in this moment, to dismiss all of this talk reflexively—to see this as little more than a form of tech marketing
Or conversely, it’s easy to believe it all uncritically
But my guests today have a different framework from which to process this moment, both in Silicon Valley and in the rest of the world

In their new book, End Times Fascism , the writers Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor offer up an idea that what we’ve seen from tech leaders in the last decade—from the AI build-out to the tech leaders’ pivot to supporting and working with Donald Trump—is all part of a broader movement of politicians and titans of industry trying to consolidate power in a moment of global instability
That this movement is, in meaningful ways, circular
For example, the tech tools create the conditions for chaos, and then those same leaders capitalize on the chaos
Klein is a New York Times best-selling author and a professor of climate justice who has been interrogating corporate power for decades
Astra Taylor is a writer, documentary filmmaker, and an activist
Together their argument is an attempt to explain a theory of power here in this turbulent decade, and how it builds off of and is different from the previous eras
But I really wanted to bring them on to zero in specifically on the “end times” part of their argument
Because whatever you think about what’s going on with our tech leaders, it seems very clear that the industry has adopted a zealous, and even religious, attitude in recent years
Promises of both utopian salvation and apocalyptic destruction are now commonplace
Silicon Valley is currently enamored with and terrified by the prospect that they are building God
They’re asking the rest of us to have faith: to put our trust in the technology and in them
But what world are they really trying to build here? And how did we get here? Klein and Taylor join me now to talk about it all
Naomi Klein, Astra Taylor: Welcome to Galaxy Brain
Warzel: So I wanna just start straight off with definitions here
Let’s start with defining end-times fascism and also how it both iterates on and is different from previous forms of fascism
Taylor: We subscribe to a view of fascism as something that didn’t just emerge as a kind of rupture in Europe in the 20th century, but something as a through line
So fascism is a form of far-right reactionary politics that uses democracy against itself, that creates kind of vertical alliances between corporate and political elites

It is an elite-led right-wing movement, and creates kind of solidarities with a group—classes of people we describe as the “injured powerful.” And so end-times fascism is our term for a form of fascism that is in dialogue, that is responsive to novel planetary-scale crises
So Hitler and Mussolini did not know a world with atomic weapons
That’s something that changes the nature of what it means to be human—the fact that we can cause that kind of annihilation
It was concentrated then, but now is even more kind of globally connected and concentrated in the hands of single individuals, like someone like Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire
We also live in a world that is being destabilized by climate change
So, you know, the fascists of yore understood pollution in the sense of something localized, but they didn’t understand the way we’re altering the chemistry of the planet
That is a huge factor in our analysis, and of course now
All these threats are being compounded by artificial intelligence

And today’s fascists are responding to these very real risks by basically accelerating, by slamming their foot on the gas and basically deciding that they’ll protect their in-group, and believing that they’ll be safe no matter what
So that’s why we see, you know, all of these high-tech lavish bunkers and this drive to fortress the nation
So fascism is always a response to real crises
It’s always a response to threats from the left, threats of redistribution
But the nature of the threats that we’re facing have changed
And we have all changed, I think, in response to these crises

title: An Anti-Marriage Marriage Movie
excerpt: The new film Wicker is, first and foremost, a love story
body: The new film Wicker is, first and foremost, a love story
And I need to acknowledge this promptly: It is a love story about a woman who falls for a person-shaped basket
Olivia Colman’s character, who is known to the audience only as Fisherwoman, is a classic spinster
She sells her smelly haul in town, tolerates taunts from her small-minded neighbors, and then retreats to her ramshackle cottage, where she spends evenings alone by the fire

But then a local artisan fashions her a husband: a doting, affectionate man (?) whose generosity and sexual aptitude easily compensate for the fact that he is, in fact, made of natural plant fibers. (Basket guy is played by Alexander Skarsgård, not that he’s recognizable under this many prosthetics.) As much as Wicker is a romance, though, it’s also a cautionary tale about marriage
The village in this film—which is directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, and based on a short story by Ursula Wills—is chock-full of miserable spouses
Bakerwoman and her husband aren’t having sex
Bottlewasher and his wife are , and she appears to be bored out of her mind during the act

When Tailor’s ambitious wife suggests that she might travel to set up new posts for the business, he scoffs at the notion that she’d do anything more than wear their garments around town and look pretty

Early in the movie, a young couple performs a wedding tradition: The officiant commands the man to place a heavy metal collar around his bride’s neck, a “symbol of lifelong duty.” As he struggles to clasp it, she gasps for air
The conventions of matrimony, for this community, are literally suffocating
Wicker asks what it would take to make the institution freeing instead—or whether marriage is simply incompatible with the kind of love that is expansive rather than constraining
Fisherwoman and her husband offer one strange, touching model
Their marriage is unique, and not only because he is, once again, an actual basket
There’s also the fact that she works for pay and he doesn’t, which doesn’t go unnoticed about town. (Not much does.) Most radically, he actually respects her, and makes it known

When they marry, someone asks where the collar is, and she responds, “We won’t be needing that.” [ Read: The existential terror of monogamy ] The presence of a loving pair in the village is totally destabilizing

The women start asking more of their husbands, who don’t appreciate the nudge. (One man grumbles about wives now seeking, for some reason, expressions of gratitude.) In a big group dance, the townspeople follow strictly choreographed steps—and they’re scandalized to see Fisherwoman and her mate creating their own moves, gazing into each other’s eyes, holding each other and swaying in the sun
Everyone seems to envy the couple their happiness and also to despise them for it
It’s as if these townspeople thought they had to live according to norms they never much liked
Now that they see that another way is possible, their own wretched and arbitrary inertia is revealed
If marriage is a mechanism of repression in Wicker , then love is a tool of liberation, capable of upending social order
That’s not an outrageous idea, however silly the movie is: The social scientist Alice Evans has tracked how romantic love, across history and nations, has driven gender equality
A besotted straight man is especially likely to see women as deserving of rights and dignity
But the film also warns that devotion is not enough, on its own, to resist the stultifying power of convention

When some men in a bar accuse the wicker husband of making their wives suddenly unsatisfied, he asks Baker: “Do you love your wife?” Baker responds that he does, and for a brief moment, he talks about her tenderly
Soon, though, the men go back to their griping
And eventually, even Fisherwoman starts succumbing to petty possessiveness
She gets paranoid about infidelity and treats her poor, hunky stick pile unkindly
You might go into a marriage starry-eyed, the film knows, and still grow complacent or controlling
Wicker is, I think, a good fit for this moment of romantic ambivalence
On the one hand, a large share of singles say they want to marry someday
On the other hand, many of them don’t know how or when they’ll achieve that goal
Some are struggling to find the right partner
Others are busy applying for jobs in an unforgiving market, or saving endlessly for a house they may never be able to afford
On average, people are marrying later and less

So young adults especially are being pushed to think critically about traditional milestones, if only because they’re not hitting them. [ Read: The bots that women use in a world of unsatisfying men ] Fisherwoman is an eccentric middle-aged woman in a tunic smeared with seafood guts, yet she might be a relatable protagonist for plenty of Zoomers: In the beginning of the movie, she mocks marriage, but only because she feels shut out of it

She both longs for romance and fears the vulnerability it requires—perhaps a particularly resonant conundrum now, when a great chunk of Gen Z seems to fear rejection and crave security . “I had such a simple life,” Fisherwoman cries to her husband. “It was nothing special, but I knew it
Now you have my heart.” One might worry that Wicker , with all of its rather unsubtle critiques of marriage, could further discourage romance-wary viewers
But as much as it’s skeptical of matrimony—and cynical about some of its characters—this is a film that roots for connection
It argues for fighting against the pull of culture and habit and convenience, day after day, to see your partner not as your belonging but as their own person

excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on
Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely
Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please

Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really? In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades
From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download

So stay tuned! In the biotech world, you can’t see everything —Jessica Hamzelou Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative
This is why it left me questioning how we cover science
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter
Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday
Help choose our next Roundtables topic Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters
Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon

( Nature ) + Companies are planning gene-edited babies. ( NYT $) + It’s also illegally felled 250,000 trees in Finland for a data center. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe

Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed
The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education
Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing . —Corey S

body: Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—journalists who interviewed her in her prime later admitted she had fooled them completely

Peer review isn't a perfect safety net: Science's built-in fact-checking system has real cracks—10,000 papers were retracted in 2023 alone, and preprint servers, press releases, and social media now routinely bypass it

Reporters face the same vulnerability as investors: Even seasoned science journalists rely on trust and expert opinion to vet claims, raising an uncomfortable question: how confident can anyone really be that they wouldn't have fallen for it too " data-chronoton-post-id="1147610" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  I went in not really knowing what to expect
I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!)

I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19
She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014
Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old
Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work
Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead
MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015
Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016
That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors
She began serving her sentence in May 2023
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children
I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film
As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups
I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people
And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out
Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind
Will anyone believe her? I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence
And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator
You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind
At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat

Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie? But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015

Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022
If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all? One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data

Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification
Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process
You should be able to trust published scientific papers
Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance
Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis
Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always
There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence
Many papers ultimately end up with corrections

title: Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories
url:
<title>Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767705/original/file-20261022-50-phtlmm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2%2C0%2C5994%2C3996&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Millions of deceased family members are gone but not forgotten by the living.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/scattered-vintage-black-and-white-photographs-depicting-people-and-scenes-EkZMVC_XQ-0">Wolfgang Vrede/Unsplash</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.</p>

<p>Present in memory and tradition, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-soc-090324-035534">dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors</a> long after they die. Recent survey data shows that <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/08/23/many-americans-report-interacting-with-dead-relatives-in-dreams-or-other-ways/">almost 44% of Americans report</a> that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone.</p>

<p>Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population. <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=t-47vMAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">As demographers</a>, <a href="http://scholar.google.com/citations?user=x0hHFh8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">we typically study</a> the living. But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like?</p>

<h2>Characterizing an unusual population</h2>

<p>Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes. In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231261474337">estimate the size and age distribution</a> of the currently living population’s deceased relatives. We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children.</p>

<p>To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called <a href="http://www.zagheni.net/uploads/3/4/4/7/34477700/microsimulation_in_demographic_research.pdf">demographic microsimulations</a>. This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans. The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad. </p>

<p>Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026.</p>

<p><iframe id="ku0Ln" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ku0Ln/5/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Bar chart shows the number of deceased in living people's memories is much greater than the number of people currently alive"></iframe></p>

<p>Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions. We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them.</p>

<p>Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population. For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals. As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead.</p>

<p>And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death. We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones. Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age.</p>

<h2>Deceased relatives of today’s Americans</h2>

<p>Our results included several key findings.</p>

<p>First, the deceased relative population is large. Our model estimated that the living Black and white populat,ion <a href="https://doi.org/10.18128/D010.V16.0">representing about 217 million people</a>, had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231261474337">755 million ties to deceased close relatives</a>. That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population. For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered. </p>

<p>Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago. That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths. </p>

<p><iframe id="opqMj" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/opqMj/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="a roughly bell-shaped line graph shows years of birth along the horizontal access and millions of people along the vertical axis"></iframe></p>

<p>Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/tricks-or-treats-goes-singular-1446228817">took hold in the U.S</a>. Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals. These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living.</p>

<p>The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors. Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days.</p>

<p>These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population. By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292342/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum

<title>UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum</title>
    <content type="html"><p>For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.</p>

<p>Under Israeli and American pressure, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted in August to end the mandate establishing <a href="https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/whatsinblue/2025/08/un-interim-force-in-lebanon-unifil-vote-on-final-mandate-renewal-and-drawdown.php">the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL</a>.</p>

<p>It means the 7,565 members of UNIFIL deployed in Lebanon – <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-troop-contributing-countries">representing about 46 countries</a> – will depart the country no later than Dec. 31, 2026.</p>

<p>The end of the U.N. presence comes at a pivotal time. Israel and Lebanon have already held <a href="https://zoryaninstitute.org/scholar-corner/lebanon-israel-are-the-negotiations-dead-or-just-stalled/">seven rounds of negotiations</a> aimed at bringing a lasting peace to a region that has suffered from decades of conflict. </p>

<p>Brokered by the United States, these talks that led to the signing of the <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/06/trilateral-framework-between-the-united-states-of-america-the-state-of-israel-and-the-republic-of-lebanon">Trilateral Framework in June 2026</a> call for the disarmament of Hezbollah, the Israeli withdrawal from all Lebanese lands and the settlement of all disputes over borders. Yet all of these conditions are still some way off from completion – and <a href="https://theconversation.com/hezbollah-degraded-weakened-but-not-yet-disarmed-destabilizes-lebanon-once-again-277327">beset by a series of barriers</a>.</p>

<p>As such, the departure of the United Nations peacekeeping forces raises serious concerns. The potential for a security vacuum looms large in south Lebanon, especially given that <a href="https://qna.org.qa/en/news/news-details?id=israeli-forces-launch-fresh-attacks-in-southern-lebanon&amp;date=6/10/2026">Israel continues to bomb Lebanon</a> despite a <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/04/ten-day-cessation-of-hostilities-to-enable-peace-negotiations-between-israel-and-lebanon">ceasefire that has nominally been in place since April 16, 2026</a>. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mireille-rebeiz-1503505">scholar of Middle East Studies</a>, I know that UNIFIL has never been a permanent solution. But I fear that its termination creates more problems than it solves, especially when there are no clear replacements or post-UNIFIL security arrangements in place. </p>

<h2>The UN in Lebanon</h2>

<p>While the U.N. had had an <a href="https://peacekeeping.un.org/sites/default/files/past/unogilbackgr.html">on-the-ground presence in Lebanon to handle civil strife since the 1950s</a>, its role in mediating between Lebanon and Israel started later.</p>

<p>In 1978, after a series of attacks on Israel organized by Palestinian fighters in Lebanon, Israel invaded and occupied the south in what was known as <a href="https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/wars-and-operations/operation-litani/">Operation Litani</a>. As a result, the United Nations Security Council <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-timeline">established UNIFIL</a> to monitor Israel’s withdrawal from south Lebanon and to restore peace at the Lebanese–Israeli border.</p>

<p>Israel’s occupation of south Lebanon lasted <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2000/may/24/israelandthepalestinians.lebanon">more than two decades</a>. Following its withdrawal on May 25, 2000, the U.N. set the <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/02/1166875">Blue Line</a> – a 75-mile (120 km) demarcation line created for the practical purpose of confirming Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon. It was not an official border but a buffer zone monitored by the U.N. peacekeepers.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>UNFIL and the Blue Line served as geographic and diplomatic focal points in the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/2006-Lebanon-War">2006 war</a> between <a href="https://theconversation.com/does-hezbollah-represent-lebanon-and-what-impact-will-the-death-of-longtime-leader-hassan-nasrallah-have-240062">Hezbollah</a> – an Iranian-backed militia operating from Lebanon – and Israel. </p>

<p>Resolution 1701 of the Security Council, which brought an end to the 2006 war, <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-timeline">dramatically expanded the UNIFIL role in Lebanon</a>; the number of troops went from 2,000 to 15,000 authorized military personnel.</p>

<p>Its mandate also changed to include monitoring the ceasefire and documenting its violations, coordinating with Lebanon’s military and functioning as the only direct communication channel between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. UNIFIL also offered humanitarian aid to the affected civilian population of south Lebanon. </p>

<p>Yet UNIFIL’s role never altered the basic lack of peace on the Israeli-Lebanese border. Over 50 years, <a href="https://theconversation.com/israeli-threats-to-occupy-or-annex-south-lebanon-dust-off-a-decades-old-playbook-279704">Israel invaded Lebanon numerous times</a>. And since 2000, <a href="https://theconversation.com/does-hezbollah-represent-lebanon-and-what-impact-will-the-death-of-longtime-leader-hassan-nasrallah-have-240062">Hezbollah has flourished in south Lebanon</a>. </p>

<p><iframe id="PEbmQ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/PEbmQ/7/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of Lebanon"></iframe></p>

<h2>A checkered history of interventions</h2>

<p>As UNIFIL prepares to depart, it’s unclear what will fill the looming security vacuum. It could be filled by non-U.N. troops, but Lebanon’s past shows the risks inherent to international peacekeeping missions. </p>

<p>In 1982, after Israel invaded Lebanon and occupied Beirut with the intention of eliminating the Palestinian militant threat, Lebanese authorities called on Western powers for help. In August, the governments of the U.S., France, Italy and the United Kingdom created a <a href="https://www.history.navy.mil/browse-by-topic/wars-conflicts-and-operations/middle-east/lebanon.html">multinational peacekeeping force</a> designed to restore peace and stop the fighting between the Lebanese, Palestinians and Israelis. </p>

<p>But on <a href="https://www.marines.mil/News/Marines-TV/videoid/634642/dvpTag/Beirut/">Oct. 23, 1983</a>, the multinational peacekeeping force was the target of a dual suicide attack that killed 241 American service members and 58 French paratroopers.  </p>

<p>To this day, the attack – claimed by the pro-Iranian <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/1983-Beirut-barracks-bombings">Islamic Jihad</a> – remains the <a href="https://www.arlingtoncemetery.mil/Explore/Monuments-and-Memorials/Beirut-Barracks">deadliest single-day incident for the U.S. Marine Corps</a> since the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945. </p>

<p>In addition to Israel, interventions in Lebanon have also come from another neighboring country.</p>

<p>In 1976, the Syrian military intervened during Lebanon’s civil war to put an end to sectarian violence. Nearly three decades of occupation followed, and troops were withdrawn only following the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-60691507">assassination of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005</a> and the subsequent <a href="https://nvdatabase.swarthmore.edu/content/lebanese-campaign-democracy-independence-intifada-or-cedar-revolution-2005">Cedar Revolution</a>.</p>

<h2>What next for Lebanon</h2>

<p>With the absence of an internal Lebanese consensus, the arrival of any international peacekeeping force to replace the exiting UNIFIL will be perceived by many Lebanese as a top-down imposition. </p>

<p>Moreover, the situation on the ground makes it dangerous for any international force to successfully operate. Israel is reportedly occupying <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/israel-expansion-maps/">over 10% of Lebanon’s territories</a>, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cge41d19gq9o">including</a> multiple permanent bases and outposts in southern Lebanese territory. </p>

<p>Hezbollah, meanwhile, <a href="https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/lebanon-hezbollah-leader-reaffirms-refusal-to-disarm-vows-continued-resistance-against-israel/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XU0hCQzExOTAwNDM">refuses to disarm</a>.  </p>

<p>Finally, the fate of Lebanon-Israel <a href="https://zoryaninstitute.org/scholar-corner/lebanon-israel-are-the-negotiations-dead-or-just-stalled/">direct negotiations is unclear</a>. Recently, the countries held military talks in Florida, but <a href="https://www.naharnet.com/stories/323237-little-expected-from-lebanon-israel-military-talks-in-florida/print">little is expected from them</a>.</p>

<p>Yet a number of efforts are ongoing despite the difficult circumstances surrounding UNIFIL’s withdrawal. On June 25, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced an “<a href="https://www.elysee.fr/en/emmanuel-macron/2026/06/25/franco-italian-joint-statement#">international coalition to support Lebanon</a>” to reinforce Lebanon’s sovereignty and help prevent a security vacuum in south Lebanon.  </p>

<p>In parallel, the <a href="https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/12/eu-agrees-new-security-mission-in-lebanon-as-un-peacekeepers-prepare-to-leave">European Union Foreign Ministers</a> approved a new civilian-military mission aimed at advising and training the Lebanese military and police personnel. </p>

<p>But these appear to be limited operations that aren’t designed to replace UNIFIL. </p>

<p>U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has previously <a href="https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/us-should-not-encourage-syria-enter-lebanon">proposed that Syria enter Lebanon</a> to help end the violence and execute “a surgical attack on Hezbollah.”</p>

<p>But given the past experience of Syrian occupation, this proposal would certainly not be welcomed by the Lebanese people.</p>

<h2>Remaining questions</h2>

<p>Although Lebanese security is a paramount concern regarding the impending withdrawal of UNIFIL, it’s not the only potential risk.</p>

<p>UNIFIL <a href="https://english.aawsat.com/arab-world/5331838-end-unifil-mission-impacts-hundreds-jobs-south-lebanon">employs many Lebanese civilians and is a steady consumer of local goods and services</a>. It also provides humanitarian aid to the region. </p>

<p>And the departure of UNIFIL may further erode Lebanon sovereignty by opening the door for the sharing of security by neighbors – and former occupiers – Syria and Israel.</p>

<p>This is all the more worrying given that the <a href="https://www.thenationalnews.com/opinion/comment/2026/03/24/theres-only-so-much-lebanons-army-can-do-against-hezbollah-it-needs-to-make-every-move-count/">Lebanese armed forces</a> are poorly trained, have a poor record as a fighting force and will be susceptible to attacks from Hezbollah fighters and sympathizers, which might trigger sectarian violence in the country. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man in a blue helmet holds a large gun" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A UNIFIL peacekeeper  in South Lebanon in 1985.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/unifil-in-south-lebanon-news-photo/948111474?phrase=UNIFIL&amp;adppopup=true">Roland Neveu/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the vacuum left by U.N. forces, some Lebanese military personnel might simply decide that opposing Hezbollah is too risky altogether.</p>

<p>All of these factors make what comes next for Lebanon after UNIFIL’s departure as opaque as it is worrying for those concerned about the country’s well-being. </p>

<p>For the sake of Lebanese sovereignty, the twin goals of disarming Hezbollah and ensuring Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory remain paramount. Yet it’s unclear who will take on those duties absent a stronger Lebanese state.</p>

<p>For all of its inability to prevent wars, invasions and violations of ceasefires, UNIFIL’s presence guaranteed a degree of Lebanese sovereignty over its lands and served as a reminder of the international community’s commitment to peace in the region. An effective replacement force would at least have to do the same.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293159/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767981/original/file-20261023-50-hmz6ge.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=164%2C657%2C4236%2C2824&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">PHP is a key building block of most websites.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/conceptual-image-of-geometric-blocks-royalty-free-image/1363978452?phrase=plain%20building%20blocks%20one%20red%20block">Richard Drury/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/php2shell-vulnerability-what-is-it-and-is-your-data-at-risk.html">to fix a vulnerability</a> in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings <a href="https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Press-Releases-Statements/Press-Release-View/Article/4630238/nsa-advisory-critical-patches-recommended-for-php-vulnerabilities/">from the U.S. National Security Agency</a>, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors. </p>

<p>A researcher at <a href="https://calif.io/">Calif</a>, a security research firm, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/cybersecurity/ai-just-found-a-bug-that-puts-up-to-70-of-the-worlds-websites-at-risk-fd0902ea">found the flaw in August 2026</a> using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, <a href="https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/hackers-got-a-four-day-head-start-on-epic-php2shell-vulnerability/">hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it</a>.</p>

<p>The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?</p>

<h2>PHP: The foundation of the web</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.php.net/">PHP</a> is a programming language that <a href="https://www.britannica.com/technology/PHP">powers most websites</a>. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/what-is-php-why-did-it-take-government-websites-offline-2026-10-21/">around 70% of websites</a> run on PHP.</p>

<p>PHP operates on a web server <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/mongodb.overview.php">in two main parts</a>: the core PHP system – the engine and <a href="https://technav.ieee.org/topic/runtime-library/">runtime libraries</a> – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/introduction.php">produce the output</a> your web browser displays.  </p>



<h2>The vulnerability</h2>

<p>The current security issue sits directly <a href="https://www.abstract.security/blog/php2shell-critical-php-rce-vulnerabilities-cve-2026-109618-and-cve-2026-109619">in the core PHP system</a> and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.</p>

<p>This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.</p>

<p>This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/K8EXJIDk-K4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How PHP2Shell works.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>AI: A double-edged sword</h2>

<p>What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.</p>

<p>This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.</p>

<p>However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities. </p>

<p>This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching">patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities</a>. </p>

<h2>Should you worry?</h2>

<p>Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/what-is-php-why-did-it-take-government-websites-offline-2026-10-21/">rely on PHP-based systems</a>. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.</p>

<p>PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer. </p>

<p>However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.</p>

<p>The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294999/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: PHP is a key building block of most websites

Richard Drury/DigitalVision via Getty Images Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites
The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S
National Security Agency , cybersecurity agencies and software vendors
A researcher at Calif , a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI
The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP
However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it
The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites
So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry? PHP: The foundation of the web PHP is a programming language that powers most websites

For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons
Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts : the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website
When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays
The vulnerability The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses
When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system
In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website
This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code
The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable
Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools
From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability
This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website
Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data
AI: A double-edged sword What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered
This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it
This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity
For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code
Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days
These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development
The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it
However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities

The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively
AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities
Should you worry? Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version
If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities
