title: Can Trump block the Alaska Senate election?
excerpt: Dan Sullivan (R-AK) at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on October 13, 2026. | Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff
body: Dan Sullivan (R-AK) at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on October 13, 2026. | Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is getting a head start on litigating the midterms.  What’s happening? The administration is asking a federal district court in Alaska to potentially block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, should incumbent Sen

Dan Sullivan, a Republican, lose to his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola.  It’s the first major lawsuit of the 2026 midterms aimed at directly challenging the results, and very likely a sign of things to come after polls close on November 3
What is the administration arguing? Sullivan is currently in a close race against Peltola, a former US representative who polls suggest may hold a slight lead
But the race is complicated by the presence of a second Dan Sullivan, Daniel J
According to the lawsuit, which names Alaska’s state elections director and several state elections entities as defendants, the election could be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J

Sullivan.”  The suit asks that “Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” which it defines as a loss by the incumbent Sullivan in the event that the other Sullivan attracts enough votes to alter the outcome of the election.  What’s the context? The second Dan Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot has already been litigated

After he was initially disqualified from the ballot, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he should be included, and he finished third in the state’s August primary (the top four vote-getters appear on Alaska’s general election ballot)
How worried about this should I be? For now, not very

Trump filing lawsuits disputing election results was all but inevitable, even if it’s surprising to see him start this early.  None of that means he’ll succeed: Trump and his allies filed dozens of election lawsuits in 2020 and were largely laughed out of court. (Plus, this particular lawsuit has been assigned to a judge appointed by President Barack Obama.) And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy Friday! Here’s some good news to add to a recent string of encouraging headlines about cancer treatment: A new vaccine may reduce the risk of melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, by more than 40 percent, according to the Washington Post
You can read all about it here with a gift link
Thanks for reading, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: How worried should I be about the AI hacking panic and “Black October”?
excerpt: An illustration shows a padlock in front of binary code on a laptop screen. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained ,
body: An illustration shows a padlock in front of binary code on a laptop screen. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained , a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

Are we living through “Black October”? Maybe, according to cybersecurity experts who are raising the alarm about AI’s increasingly sophisticated and far-reaching hacking abilities.  This week alone has seen a string of alarming incidents where AI uncovered previously unknown security flaws deep in the infrastructure of the internet

The most concerning involves something called PHP —  a programming language that, according to The Atlantic , is used by “as much as 70 percent of websites.” Cybersecurity researchers used AI to locate a major security breach in the technology
It’s the kind of thing that, when it’s working, is practically invisible

When it stops, though, you really notice it: Government websites in the UK and Europe briefly went down earlier this week after the PHP vulnerability was discovered, as did some sites in the Wikipedia family, the Internet Archive, and many others
The outages weren’t actually the result of a hack, but rather preventative action as web engineers took sites down to fix the vulnerability before it was exploited

But not every PHP-like issue will necessarily be uncovered before it can be exploited by someone using AI tools less ethically, and older websites relying on PHP might go unpatched.  The problem doesn’t stop there, either: Concern is also rising around AI cybersecurity risks to ubiquitous conveniences like online banking

As Axios reported on Thursday , banks are detecting more and more “unauthorized third-party AI agents ” operating inside of their systems.  Those agents are mostly unauthorized by the banks , Axios explains — the holders of the bank account might have given them permission — but it still creates a security risk that executives described as “horrifying,” in part because banks can’t necessarily tell if an agent doesn’t have permission.  It’s a lot to take in, all of it moving extremely quickly, and it’s hard to tell what any of us can do about it as AI labs continue to forge ahead with ever more competent AI models and agents
Luckily, my colleague Adam Clark Estes has some simple recommendations to shore up your own cybersecurity
How do I respond right now? One problem with hackers — even those that happen to be AI agents — is that they can be unpredictable
You won’t know to, say, lock down your Quest Diagnostics records before a breach happens
But whenever you find yourself wondering if your data is safe, that’s a good time to double check that you’ve at least covered your bases
The National Cybersecurity Alliance, a nonprofit dedicated to the safe use of technology, maintains a list of basic online safety practices that everyone should follow
In no particular order, here’s what to pay attention to now: Keep your guard up
AI makes it difficult to know the difference between humans and robots
So be extra careful to avoid engaging in potential phishing scams
Don’t reply to unknown texts, and do due diligence on texts or emails that look like they’re from people you know but just seem off
Don’t give out personal info over the phone, even if it sounds like it’s someone you know
They might be scammers using AI to clone a loved one’s voice
Yes, it’s annoying to pause your phone or computer use for a few minutes to update your software, but this is one of the best ways to get rid of vulnerabilities
Companies like Apple and Google employ huge teams of security experts to spot these in their software and fix them with software updates
Use a password manager or, even better, passkeys
Each of your online accounts should have a unique password that’s at least 16 characters
Yes, it’s impossible to remember that many passwords, so you should also use a password manager like 1Password or the app built into your iPhone or Android device
Just in case you don’t already do it, make sure you use multifactor or two-step authentication for all your accounts, including email and social media
It can be annoying to type in a code or check your email while logging in, but hackers, including AI agents, will have a much harder time getting into your accounts if you take this step
Taking all these measures is not a one-time affair
You have to be vigilant in keeping yourself safe online
Security experts have a term for this that’s almost too specific: cyber hygiene
Like brushing your teeth or taking a shower, take good care of your online life, and do it often
One link for later ➨ Is it still possible to ban gerrymandering? The current US Supreme Court is very, very hostile to getting politics out of congressional map-making
But if Democrats win back power, that doesn’t mean they shouldn’t try
My colleague Ian Millhiser gamed out how they could do it in a way that survives the Court — as well as some approaches that almost certainly wouldn’t fly
But, he writes, the real trick will be finding a solution that functions the way Congress wants it to and can’t be exploited by mapmakers

Before you go… Did you know… that the disease multiple sclerosis is misdiagnosed with surprising frequency ? As many as 15 percent of diagnoses could be false positives — including that of Christina Applegate, who found out this week that she does not have MS despite a 2021 diagnosis
Today’s trivia: Which noble gas is radioactive and has the chemical symbol Rn? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked what the plural was for multiple Toyota hybrids
That would be Prii, which Toyota officially confirmed in 2011 after holding a vote.

title: Should you let a chatbot manage your money?
excerpt: A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money
body: A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money
I can say that personal finance wasn’t dinner table conversation in my house, and even as I went off to college and started fending for myself, it was almost a taboo subject

When it came to money, people either had it or they didn’t, and you definitely didn’t talk about it.  Maybe this is why the average American isn’t exactly fluent in personal finance, and the situation is getting worse
Americans can only answer about 50 percent of basic questions about borrowing, savings, and risk on a financial literacy survey, according to a 2026 study by TIAA , a retirement services company
About a third of those surveyed said they have a hard time making ends meet and are debt-constrained
These figures have remained relatively unchanged for nearly a decade , but dropped to their lowest level in this year’s study
It makes sense: It’s hard to learn about money when it’s not taught in schools, and it’s such an intensely private topic

It’s also hard to make good financial decisions when you’re one of the growing number of American households struggling to pay bills , repay debts, and save for the future — and feeling very stressed about it
In a perfect world, each of us could sit down with a financial adviser to get help — but most of us can’t afford that

Instead, average Americans tend to find personal finance tips on TikTok, in Reddit threads, by watching Suze Orman on YouTube or How to Get Rich on Netflix, or by Googling their questions.  Now we have AI tools, too.  With access to an internet’s worth of information and financial advice, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI chatbots can answer any question you ask

They can help you put together a basic budget or, armed with your bank statements and the details of your student loans and your retirement accounts, tailor solutions to your specific situation. Or, at least, that’s the promise
Key takeaways More people are turning to AI for financial advice : One in five Americans have used AI to help manage their money, and some experts think chatbots could be better than the status quo

AI works best if you know what questions to ask : Those with basic financial literacy will be able to make the most of these tools, while those without it — who might need help the most — could be led astray
Better advice comes with greater risks : Sharing your financial information with a chatbot helps personalize its recommendations
This raises privacy concerns, so you might want to delete your data when you’re done
Think of AI as a financially savvy friend : Chatbots can answer money questions you might be embarrassed to ask someone else and use that context to help build your budget
AI could create a more utopian, more equitable future, where reliable, hyper-personalized advice is just a prompt or two away for people who can’t afford to meet with an expert in real life
But machines are built by people, and there’s good reason to be concerned that these machines will simply replicate the biases and disparities built into our current system

Here’s what experts say about how to make the most of these tools — and how to think about all of the inherent risks of uploading a lot of personal financial information to a chatbot or, worse, giving an AI agent the keys to your bank account

The steep rise, risks, and rewards of AI financial advisers Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used AI tools like ChatGPT for financial advice, and close to 25 percent for Gen Z adults and millennials have tried it, according to an August Gallup poll

These numbers could tick up too: In October, OpenAI started rolling out a dedicated personal finance tool to its ChatGPT Free and Go users in the United States, which effectively means anyone can try it

ChatGPT Finances lets you securely connect your bank account to the tool using a platform called Plaid , and then you can basically have a conversation with the chatbot about your real-time finances down to the penny
It’s like an AI-powered Mint ( RIP ) that you can talk to directly
Regardless of where you encounter a chatbot or how much data you give it, experts say these tools could genuinely help improve financial literacy
You can talk to them about money problems you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family, or ask questions and receive actionable, personalized information
There are real upsides to using AI this way
Taha Choukhmane , an associate professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management, has been studying outcomes when people turn to chatbots for financial advice

In general, these AI tools give pretty good advice, and that advice gets better as people become more practiced in asking the right question , according to research he published earlier this year.  “We were actually quite surprised that relative to the status quo, the average American would be better off if they were to follow the advice,” Choukhmane told me

But he added a caveat: “Just following the advice without understanding the advice puts you at risk of not fully understanding the risk.” But you shouldn’t trust everything a chatbot tells you and should verify everything before making any decisions.  Chatbot advice has some significant limitations
The finance industry has a vested interest in steering you toward certain ways of managing your money, and that typically means selling you products, like loans
If you’ve ever searched for personal finance tips on Google, you’ve probably noticed that a lot of the top results come from banks and other financial institutions
This is by design, according to John Campbell , an economics professor at Harvard

But because AI is aggregating all of that advice, the specific influences and possible bias is less obvious.  “AI is very promising for providing low-cost financial advice in plain English that will arguably be better than what many people would be able to do on their own,” said Campbell, who’s also the co-author of Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone . “One caveat is that chatbot advice is quite likely — unless a model has been carefully trained — to reflect the average of whatever’s being posted on the internet, and that may or may not be first-rate advice.” An example Campbell gives is the question of when to start taking Social Security benefits

While you’re eligible at age 62, many economists agree that you should delay your benefits, which, based on the way the government calculates your monthly payouts , will allow you to enjoy much higher benefits later in life
But paid financial advisers can recommend starting as early as possible, since waiting longer reduces the amount of money that needs to be managed, which reduces the adviser’s fees
That means there’s a lot of conflicting advice online , much of it supplied by the finance industry

And that’s the information used to train AI models. “The advice is much more mixed,” Campbell said. “And so if a chatbot is learning from that, it may not actually give the best advice.” It can be hard to recognize bad advice anywhere in life, but especially when you’re talking to a machine that’s programmed to please you

A chatbot could encourage you to consider a balance transfer, to lean in on credit card rewards, or to refinance your mortgage — all decisions with upsides and downsides for you, but definite upsides for banks — without you realizing how much of its training data comes from the finance industry selling these products
What’s worse is that if you do end up taking bad advice, it might be years before you realize it
You won’t know that you refinanced a mortgage at a bad time until a better time comes along

title: Wild animals can’t vote. Here’s where they’re on the ballot anyway.
excerpt: A male Northern Bobwhite Quail forages for seeds on the ground in south Texas. | Jon G
body: A male Northern Bobwhite Quail forages for seeds on the ground in south Texas. | Jon G
Fuller/VWPics/Universial Images Group via Getty When millions of voters fill out their ballots in November, they won’t just be choosing elected representatives

Many states are offering the chance to impact conservation and wildlife as well, through ballot measures focused on things like dedicating more money to habitat protection or mitigating the impacts of climate change
One could even reshape wildlife management in one of the country’s most picturesque mountain states — and also lead to the indiscriminate deaths of all kinds of wild animals
And while ballot measures might seem like small potatoes in the grand scheme of electoral politics, they could have an outsized impact this year

The Trump administration has been systematically rolling back protections for endangered species, taking a hammer to longstanding pillars of climate regulation , and cutting funding to agencies like the National Park Service and National Forest Service , both of which oversee vast stretches of wildlife habitats

In many cases, states have had to step up, putting more resources into conserving the habitats and species within their borders, and ballot measures can help shape those decisions.  Here are the seven ballot measures that could transform ecosystems across the country this election:  California — Proposition 45 : Cutting pesky environmental reviews, also maybe cutting habitats   This ballot measure would shorten environmental review periods for “essential projects” like housing, water systems, clean energy, and medical facilities, among others
In a state that’s been struggling to build what it needs fast enough, this could help speed essential clean energy projects that could help slow climate change

On the other hand, reducing California Environmental Quality Act review time, as this proposition would do, could also lead to increased habitat destruction, leading advocacy organizations like the Sierra Club to oppose it.  Georgia — Amendment 1 : Tax breaks for conservation land (maybe) This amendment might seem a little in the weeds — and mostly in the interest of farmers and ranchers looking for tax breaks
But it would double (from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres) the amount of land an owner can get tax breaks from if they protect it under the state’s Conservation Use Valuation Assessment program

As Yanshu Li , an Associate Professor of Forest Economics at the University of Georgia, told me, the amendment could incentivize landowners to set aside larger tracts of their property for wildlife habitat conservation, which would benefit species like the nine-banded armadillo and the northern bobwhite quail that call these habitats home.  Massachusetts — Question 6 : A fund for nature Question 6 would create a “Nature for All Fund,” routing existing taxes on sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and money spent at golf courses to conservation
That fund could then be used on natural resource conservation, making it the first time the state has a dedicated funding source for conservation projects

Colorado — Proposition 137 : More money for restoration and wildfire prevention This proposition, similar to Massachusetts’, would direct existing sales taxes on sporting goods to a state fund dedicated to conservation and wildfire prevention
In a state where wildfires have torn through more than 2 million acres in the past decade, dozens of conservation groups are supporting this measure to protect habitats and species

Arkansas — Issue 4 : Waterworks and waterways  Here, voters are being asked to approve up to $500 million in bonds that can be used to fund water-related infrastructure projects like water treatment, waste disposal, and wetlands infrastructure

A boost to wetlands under the Arkansas proposal could help animals that live in those habitats, which are often overlooked in this region.  Rhode Island — Question 5 : New money for climate resilience and habitat protection This measure would allow for $55 million in bonds to fund environmental and recreational projects
The largest chunk of this change — $25 million — would go to helping to protect the state from the impacts of climate change

Another $7 would be devoted to protecting Narragansett Bay and its watersheds, which would include funding to “restore natural habitats and control invasive aquatic plants,” according to the Rhode Island Current .  These ballot measures are all relatively straightforward so far, but there’s one question up to voters this fall that puts wild animals front-and-center — and is splitting hunters and anglers down an ethical centerline
Which takes us back to Colorado:  Colorado — Amendment 83 : A constitutional right to hunt…traditionally On its surface, this amendment seems fairly innocuous
It asks voters to enshrine “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” in the state’s constitution
Hunting and fishing are already big in Colorado, and they’re protected by statute, so this may not seem like a major change

But, as Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, speaking for herself, told me , neither the text of the bill nor its proponents define what “traditional methods” of hunting and fishing would be allowed under this amendment. “Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Niemiec said
Many of these practices injure or maim animals, including ones that aren’t targeted: Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf, and a lynx

All of these practices have been outlawed in Colorado over the years, either through other ballot measures or regulatory changes; in 1992, for example, Coloradans voted to ban hunting bears using bait and hounds, and four years later they banned leg-hold traps and snares.  The new amendment also continues on to propose: “establishing hunting and fishing as the preferred means of managing fish and wildlife populations.” This would leave far less room for wildlife agencies like CPW to make nuanced decisions or roll out alternative programs, like birth control or animal relocation

It also reduces their ability to take into account the preferences of people who value wildlife for reasons other than hunting.  “Biological science can inform decisions about how many animals can be killed without threatening a population,” Niemiec said. “But it can’t tell us what hunting practices are ethical, or how to balance hunting opportunities with the public’s desire to see wildlife alive — and protected from unnecessary suffering.”  The push for these constitutional protections, Niemiec told me, is part of a larger backlash against conservation groups

But in this case, it’s not as simple as hunter vs. non-hunter: Plenty of hunters and anglers support taking ethical considerations into account when making decisions about how to manage wildlife, and some hunting groups in Colorado have publicly spoken out against the amendment.  “If we’re going to enshrine anything in the Constitution, it should say we should be balancing the diversity of public interest in wildlife in all of our management decisions,” Niemiec said. “We need innovative methods, not traditional methods, if we’re going to deal with the complex challenges that our wildlife is facing moving forward in the state and throughout the country.”

title: We’ve spent decades fighting campus sexual assault. Why haven’t colleges figured it out?
excerpt: Demonstrators gather at the Washington Monument on October 8, 2026, in Washington, DC, to rally in support of a Cornell University student who alleges she was r
body: Demonstrators gather at the Washington Monument on October 8, 2026, in Washington, DC, to rally in support of a Cornell University student who alleges she was raped at a fraternity house on campus in 2024. | Michael A

McCoy for the Washington Post via Getty Images Last month, a former Cornell University student identified in court papers as “Jane Doe” sued her university and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity , alleging they raped her at the group’s house in October 2024

Cornell’s own disciplinary process for the incident had ended with two of the men expelled, two suspended and put on probation, one (who had already graduated) barred from campus, and two found not responsible but ordered to complete trainings and write reflection papers
The local district attorney declined to press charges
Since the lawsuit was filed, the DA has reopened the case and New York state officials have launched an investigation
Students have also held sit-ins, and some are calling for the university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, to resign
Cornell has suspended fraternity parties for the rest of the year
View this post on Instagram But this kind of case — and the issues it raises about campus life — are not new

Educators, students, activists, and politicians have spent decades debating how to prevent sexual assault, how to protect victims, how to balance the rights of the accused, and what to do about Greek life
At times, those conversations have resulted in significant changes to policy — which in turn have also generated backlash and brought more changes in response

Elizabeth Armstrong , a sociologist at the University of Michigan, began researching campus sexual assault in the early 2000s, embedding at a Midwestern university to understand how fraternities, alcohol, and the lack of anywhere else to go put students at risk

She has seen attention to the issue come and go in the public discourse across generations of students, often spurred by high-profile incidents like a Time magazine cover in 1991 spotlighting a first-year William & Mary student who was date raped, and a Stanford swimmer in 2016 who was sentenced to six months in jail for assaulting an unconscious woman after a frat party
I wanted to know what Armstrong makes of Cornell, and if she thinks anything is different this time

Has anything actually gotten better since the Title IX fights of the 2010s ? What do people who haven’t been on a campus in a while misunderstand about how students socialize? And what could a school like Cornell do right now, without waiting on the courts or Washington, DC? I talked to Armstrong about Greek life, what survivors of sexual assault actually want from their schools, and the reforms she thinks colleges need to be paying attention to
Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity

Could you start by sharing briefly the kind of research you’ve done on campus sexual assault? I did ethnographic and interview work at a Midwestern university, starting in 2003, and published a paper in 2006 on the organizational conditions that lead to sexual risk on campus
I later co-authored Paying for the Party: How College Maintains Inequality , a 2013 book based on that research
Were there many people talking about this back in the early 2000s? It was in something of a hiatus period
Interest in this issue essentially goes in waves
There was interest in the ’70s, then again in the late ’80s, and then there was a hiatus

My research and writing happened right before things started to build back up again with interest.  So before we get into Cornell specifically, could you paint a bit of a picture of how campus social life tends to work? Where students gather, who hosts parties, and where Greek life fits in? So the basic gist is that at four-year American residential universities, students often live in residence halls or they live off campus, or if there’s residential Greek life, they live in fraternities and sororities.  Young people like to congregate, and they like to party, to have fun, and drink, and figure out opportunities to hook up

One of the things that has emerged, particularly on campuses with fraternities that have their own houses, is that these organizations control the party resources — like the space and alcohol, and time and energy to host
So it’s hard to avoid them if you are someone who wants to party

Yes, and one of the things that’s been coming out of the discussion related to Cornell is that the pandemic really flattened the number of bars, restaurants, and cafes in Ithaca — places where people might have otherwise had opportunities to hang out
So it gave an already really dominant Greek scene even more centrality and power over the way students socialize
My next question was going to be what do people who haven’t been on a college campus in a while tend to misunderstand about the party scene, and that pandemic shift seems like an answer to that

Yes, and people often don’t understand that for a lot of first-year students, who are generally under 21 but still wanting to drink, figuring out how to get alcohol, where the parties are, where the fun is going to be, is a challenge for them

Students entering college often don’t have good resources to know what’s safe and not safe.  Yeah, and it seems like colleges just cover their eyes and deploy a don’t-ask-don’t-tell policy on underage drinking
Years ago, when I was doing more traveling and speaking on college campuses, cab drivers would be telling me how they’d deposit students drunk all the time
And if a school was religiously affiliated or anything, they would just deny that their own students were partying with alcohol at all

And so the students were just vastly more at risk than even at campuses where officials were willing to admit what actually goes on.  Based on your research of party rape, what parts of campus life do you think we should be paying attention to with Cornell and other colleges?  Here I’d bring up a book, Sexual Citizens by Jennifer Hirsch and Shamus Khan

They did ethnography at Columbia University, and they pointed out some concepts like “sexual geography” — which is this idea that you can go onto any campus and see the ways things are organized to be more risky.  They point out, for example, that if students have nowhere to socialize except in dorm rooms with beds, that’s more risky than if they had lounges or other kinds of nonsexual spaces to congregate

And like, are there fun things to do that are substance-free if people want that? Are there spaces for queer students or students of color to hang out? What are the social options, and who controls where the fun happens? That makes so much sense
If there’s no alternative, then people will go to whatever option is available, even if it’s less safe.  Yeah, and I mean it’s tricky because sometimes it’s not considered hip or cool to do that

When we were doing our observation research way back in the early 2000s, the university we were studying was trying to create some non-frat party options, and the women that we studied thought those were just hopelessly nerdy and uncool, and they didn’t want to go because they were not seen as being high-status things to do

What do you think colleges could be doing differently when it comes to parties? One thing I think that colleges could do — like now that we do have Uber and Lyft — they could get a Lyft subscription where students can call up 24/7 to get home safely from wherever they happen to be, no questions asked
That could be expensive, but it’s a lot more expensive when serious harm happens
So ensuring people can get home safely could be one measure
And Michael Roth, the president of Wesleyan, had an op-ed this week in the New York Times suggesting that universities consider making these organizations co-ed
Not abolishing them completely, but transforming them

In the moody alcoves of a lobby bar in Chicago in 2021 over French 75s, Dr
Louise King, a gynecologic surgeon, and Katie L

Watson, a bioethics professor, found themselves in conversation about a topic that had long frustrated them both: Female surgeons are consistently underpaid compared to male surgeons, even after accounting for specialty, rank, age, and other factors.  What troubled them even more was how the pay gap compounded in King’s own field
Surgeons who perform procedures that are specifically for women, like gynecological surgeries, are paid less for their services than surgeons who perform comparable surgeries for the male anatomy
Gynecologic surgeons are also predominantly women

Over the course of the conversation, Watson termed this situation “double discrimination,” a phrase that captures the overlapping dilemma of lower pay for surgeries in a specialty that is overwhelmingly female and also serves a primarily female patient population
Key takeaways Doctors are paid less for gynecologic surgeries than for similar surgeries on men
That pay gap has barely improved in the last 20 years

The value of each procedure is largely set by a committee of doctors that relies on self-reported, and sometimes inaccurate, surveys in which doctors report the skill and time their own procedures require

When doctors are paid less to treat women’s health concerns, hospitals allocate fewer resources to those services, leading to worse outcomes for women  Experts say the gap can be closed by reconsidering how gynecologic surgeries are valued and removing sex-specific billing codes
That term, which has since entered the medical literature , stuck because the problem it describes has been well documented for decades
In 1997, a group of gynecologic surgeons published a paper in the journal Gynecologic Oncology with a title that gets straight to it — “ Is Adam worth more than Eve ?” Dr

Goff, now chair of Obstetrics and Gynecology at University of Washington Medicine, and colleagues found that doctors are paid around 44 percent more for performing male-specific procedures than analogous female-specific ones.  In the three decades since, the problem hasn’t been fixed
To the contrary, it has been effectively institutionalized, built into the systems and codes that determine how surgeons bill for procedures of all kinds
Today, gynecologic or female-specific procedures are in large part still reimbursed at lower rates than male-specific procedures even when they take similar time and skill
Those disparities have consequences that extend beyond the compensation of individual doctors
When gynecological procedures don’t bring in as much money to hospitals, those same hospitals are disincentivised to offer women’s health services
That can lead to worse care for women and, crucially, fewer training opportunities for the surgeons who do that work.  But this historically persistent inequality is not a foregone conclusion
How healthcare services are billed changes all the time as procedures get reevaluated, new ones get added, and medical societies and experts push for revisions
In fact, one of the biggest changes in how maternity care is billed and reimbursed is set to take effect early next year , splitting up services for prenatal care, delivery, postpartum care, and more

While this is a long-overdue fix for obstetrics, gynecologic surgery — which covers most of a woman’s life outside of childbearing years — continues to be left out of the conversation.  And although real change will require concerted efforts, King and Watson — and other advocates who have spent years documenting this disparity — have a fairly clear sense of how to start fixing it.   How surgical procedures are valued The work of deciding how much a medical procedure is worth starts well above the head of any given doctor, medical practice, or hospital

In the United States, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a federal agency that administers healthcare and health insurance policies, sets rates for different procedures based on a metric called relative value units (RVUs)
An RVU is supposed to take into account how long a procedure takes, the skill it requires, and the intensity of work it demands
Both Medicare and private insurers consider these figures when they’re settling on reimbursement levels
If a procedure has a higher RVU, it is valued more highly, and makes more money

In a recent study, cheekily titled “ Price and Prejudice ,” researchers from the Mount Sinai Health System found that out of 55 pairs of sex-specific procedures that they evaluated in 2023, 75 percent had lower RVUs for procedures on female patients
On average, RVUs for male-specific procedures were 30 percent higher, and when those procedures were performed in a hospital or surgical center, surgeons were paid around 26 percent more
For example, doctors will often perform biopsies — taking a small sample of tissues, cells, or fluids — on both male and female genitalia to diagnose problems

In 2023, researchers found that Medicare’s standard national rate for reimbursing surgeons was $121.32 for a penile biopsy but only $65.74 for a vaginal biopsy.  Loading interactive graphic… title: Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix

body: 41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’ Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s
The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record
Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s

It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores

But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it
Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture
There is only the right solution for the business problem
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight
An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures
The constraints should determine the architecture
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments
During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion

Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements
Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload
That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern
It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost
Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another
Serving architecture influences memory utilization
Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value
This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance
During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length
As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available
Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize
Then determine if another bottleneck emerged
Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all
The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question
Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value
Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s
The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs
A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series
It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models
Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes

title: The Foundations of Scalable AI
excerpt: A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation
body: A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation
Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one

This session from MIT Technology Review’s EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic systems, into lasting value for investors

About the speaker Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard Jing Wang leads Vanguard’s Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm’s AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities

Her team drives enterprise-wide innovation, research, and delivery, enabling Vanguard to translate emerging technologies into trusted solutions that enhance client experiences, improve investor outcomes, and create measurable business value
Before her current position, Jing served in a range of leadership roles across Vanguard’s Financial Services, Workplace Solutions, International, and Corporate Services divisions
Throughout her tenure, she has led teams and enterprise initiatives that advanced strategic priorities, strengthened client outcomes, and drove business performance across the firm
She joined Vanguard in 2009 after several years as a Principal at the Boston Consulting Group

Jing earned a B.S. in Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China, a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an M.B.A. in Finance and Marketing from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania
Jing holds Series 7, 24, and 65 licenses.

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

How far can we push computing? On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued
He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size
Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance

Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.  Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing . —Volkan Gurses This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue
It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains , our series exploring the ideas shaping technology

Read more from the series .  Three things you should know about permafrost How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it
The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects
Here are three things I took away from his reporting . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
body: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one
As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says
Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know
The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use
A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve
Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them
Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling
This approach could also change how employees spend their time
Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions
Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents
Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales
With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly

As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis

This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis
Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads
After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle
By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit
They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis
Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today

Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question
And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned
As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization
We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes
There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency
In either of them, we have some processes in place
You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first
Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task
And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate
And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context

And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come

If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic

title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
url:
<title>Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766801/original/file-20261016-50-rpqs3i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Survivorship care is part of comprehensive cancer care.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/man-with-hand-on-chest-talking-with-female-medical-royalty-free-image/2185763814">Maskot/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a <a href="https://theconversation.com/prostate-cancer-treatment-is-not-always-the-best-option-a-cancer-researcher-walks-her-father-through-his-diagnosis-206975">whirlwind of decisions</a> that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time. </p>

<p>You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=DSI-14cAAAAJ">nurse and scientist</a> who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.</p>

<p>In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head &amp; Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3198">stick to treatment and be alive without cancer</a> three years after treatment.</p>

<h2>What is cancer survivorship?</h2>

<p>Clinicians and researchers consider a person a <a href="https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/coping/survivorship">cancer survivor</a> from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.</p>

<p>Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the <a href="https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cncr.70039">complex needs of a cancer survivor</a> beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Patient lying on exam table as ultrasound technician places instrument on their neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766622/original/file-20261015-50-yxa4lc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cancer care requires significant coordination across medical specialties.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-doctor-examining-a-patients-neck-by-using-an-royalty-free-image/1473904717">ljubaphoto/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.  </p>

<p>After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.</p>

<h2>Timing matters for cancer survivorship</h2>

<p>While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons <a href="https://www.facs.org/quality-programs/cancer-programs/commission-on-cancer/standards-and-resources/">Commission on Cancer</a>, hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.</p>

<p>While survivorship care can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11764-021-01128-1">ease physical and psychological issues</a> after cancer treatment, survivors often report <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/00034894231154182">significant unmet needs</a> before and during treatment.</p>

<p>In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2025.4203">treatment interruption and hospitalization</a>. These side effects often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.34861">continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of person holding hand to their neck" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766623/original/file-20261015-50-mzzlhu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Treatment for head and neck cancer can come with significant side effects.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-with-thyroid-gland-problem-royalty-free-image/1855047943">Pony Wang/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00520-025-09797-9">better quality of life and reduced symptoms</a>.</p>

<p>In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaoto.2026.3198">completing radiation finished treatment on time</a>, compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.</p>

<p>Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.</p>

<h2>Survivorship care is not universal</h2>

<p>Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.18736">receive survivorship care</a>.</p>

<p>For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/hed.26066">address psychological symptoms</a>, such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.</p>

<p>Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.18736">lack of referrals</a> can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.</p>

<h2>Thinking ahead in cancer care</h2>

<p>The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts. </p>

<p>Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients. </p>

<p>As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294431/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
